ai-at-work.title: OpenAI acquires presentation startup NextSlide
ai-at-work.excerpt: NextSlide says its team members are now working on ChatGPT.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: OpenAI bought NextSlide, a presentation software startup, and folded the team into ChatGPT development. This matters because it signals that AI companies are serious about making presentations less painful, which means your deck tools are about to get weird fast. Look, I've sat through enough PowerPoint hell to appreciate the irony: the thing that finally kills death-by-slides might be an AI that's just as capable of generating corporate nonsense, only faster.

ai-at-work.title: Forecasting the AI bubble: When scarcity turns to surplus
ai-at-work.excerpt: Artificial intelligence can be technologically transformative and still produce a capital bubble. Those two ideas are not in conflict. The bubble bursting does not require AI to fail. It only requires
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Silicon Angle is arguing that AI can be genuinely transformative while still being in a speculative bubble, and that the bubble pops not when technology fails but when supply of AI capacity outpaces actual business demand for it. For digital workplace leaders, this means the current mad rush to AI adoption might cool considerably once companies realize they've bought more capability than they can actually use profitably. My take: buckle up for the "AI winter" hangover, because nothing sobers up an executive suite faster than realizing they spent millions on AI that just sits there looking expensive.

ai-at-work.dwp_take: OpenAI disclosed that its unreleased Astra model could potentially have "critical" hacking capabilities that pose cybersecurity risks, though details remain sparse. Digital workplace leaders need to pay attention because if AI models this powerful are hitting production environments, your security posture had better be locked down tight or you'll be the next breach headline. Here's the thing though: OpenAI talking about risks before launch is actually responsible, so maybe let's see the actual details before we all panic-buy cybersecurity consulting.

ai-at-work.title: Post-quantum security deadlines force leaders to protect existing infrastructure
ai-at-work.excerpt: The post-quantum security transition is emerging as one of the most pressing challenges facing enterprise and government infrastructure, as “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks — in which adversaries
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Organizations are racing to upgrade their encryption before quantum computers become powerful enough to crack today's security standards, driven by real threats of attackers stealing encrypted data now and decrypting it later. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because your collaboration platforms, email systems, and file storage all rely on encryption that could become vulnerable, turning today's "confidential" into tomorrow's open book. The real kicker is that most teams haven't even finished their last security overhaul, and now they're being told to start planning the next one before quantum computers are even a practical threat.

tools-tech.title: Wispr moves beyond AI dictation with note-taking assistant
tools-tech.excerpt: Wispr, the startup behind dictation tool Wispr Flow, has created an AI note-taking assistant that records meetings and generates conversation summaries for users. The Wispr Flow Notetaker tool “captur
tools-tech.dwp_take: Wispr is expanding from a simple dictation tool to an AI-powered meeting recorder that automatically summarizes conversations so you're not juggling pen and paper during calls. This matters because knowledge workers spend ridiculous amounts of mental energy documenting meetings instead of actually paying attention, so automating that could free up real brainpower. That said, I'd want to see how well it actually captures context and action items before declaring this a game-changer, because plenty of AI summaries read like they were written by someone who dozed through half the meeting.

tools-tech.title: Cloudflare wants to provide the operating system for the AI-first enterprise
tools-tech.excerpt: Traditional operating systems (OS) were built to manage hardware, files, apps, and users on a device, but Cloudflare says the agentic AI era requires a whole new format. The company this week announce
tools-tech.dwp_take: Cloudflare launched an open-source, browser-based operating system designed to connect AI agents, enterprise data, and internal workflows in a single secure workspace, positioning itself as infrastructure for the AI-first enterprise. This matters to digital workplace folks because if it gains traction, it could reshape how we think about security, access control, and system architecture beyond traditional device-centric OS models. Honestly though, after 30 years watching companies chase the next big platform, I'll believe it's transformative when I see actual adoption in messy real-world enterprises, not just tech-forward early adopters.

digital-culture.title: Hiring program in energy tech sector enlists military veterans to fill data center skills gap
digital-culture.excerpt: With an unprecedented surge in demand for skilled technicians, Schneider Electric eyes talent with military experience.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Schneider Electric is actively recruiting military veterans to staff data centers as demand for skilled technicians outpaces the current labor supply in the energy tech sector. This matters to digital workplace pros because it highlights how talent shortages are forcing organizations to look beyond traditional hiring pools, which means rethinking recruitment strategies and workplace integration for non-traditional candidates. Here's the thing: if we'd been investing in technical training pipelines instead of waiting for crisis mode, we wouldn't be poaching veterans from their transition programs.

digital-culture.title: The Hottest New AI Chatbot Is Just a Guy Answering Your Questions
digital-culture.excerpt: WIRED spoke with Tucker Bryant, an artist and former Google employee who created ChatTJB to get people to reflect on the “strange moment” we’re in.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Tucker Bryant built ChatTJB, an AI chatbot that's actually just him answering questions in real time, as a commentary on our current obsession with artificial intelligence. This matters to digital workplace folks because it exposes a hard truth: we're implementing AI solutions without asking whether we actually need them, and sometimes a human on the other end does the job better. The real punchline here is that Bryant proved what we should have known all along: the technology isn't the bottleneck, the thinking is.

That said, it's beta software from a company that already makes solid infrastructure products, so this could be genuinely useful or it could be another shiny thing that needs eighteen more months of baking.

industry-news.excerpt: Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid robot can swap its own battery in under three minutes, a feature designed to reduce downtime during industrial work. The post Boston Dynamics’ Atlas Robot Can Change It

The real kicker: a machine that fixes itself is less annoying than most of my colleagues, and that's saying something.

industry-news.title: Meta Ordered to Pay $567M and Overhaul Teen Safety on Facebook, Instagram
industry-news.excerpt: Meta must pay $567 million and change Facebook and Instagram protections for minors under a New Mexico court order it plans to appeal. The post Meta Ordered to Pay $567M and Overhaul Teen Safety on Fa
industry-news.dwp_take: Meta got hit with a $567 million fine and court-ordered safety overhauls for how it handles teen users on Facebook and Instagram, though the company plans to appeal. For digital workplace professionals, this matters because it signals regulators are finally willing to impose real consequences for social platforms that treat user safety like an afterthought, which could force changes to how your organization thinks about internal collaboration tools. Personally, I've watched Meta dodge accountability for two decades, so watching a court actually make them pay feels like someone finally calling out that kid who's been cutting in line since elementary school.

industry-news.title: Samsung’s August Update Patches 56 Security Vulnerabilities Across Galaxy Devices
industry-news.excerpt: Samsung’s August 2026 Galaxy update fixes 56 Android and One UI security flaws, including critical vulnerabilities and clipboard access risks. The post Samsung’s August Update Patches 56 Security Vuln
industry-news.dwp_take: Samsung just dropped an August update that patches 56 security holes across Galaxy devices, including some nasty clipboard access vulnerabilities that could let attackers snoop on what you're copying and pasting. For anyone managing Galaxy devices across your organization, this is a mandatory install situation because clipboard access is basically handing someone the keys to sensitive data your employees are handling daily. After three decades watching security theater, I can tell you that 56 vulnerabilities in one update means Samsung's security team was either very thorough in their audit or very worried about what they'd missed.
